title: How to Grade Your Child’s IB Coursework at Home
summary: Learn how to review your child’s IB IA at home using rubric-based checks while protecting academic integrity and leaving official grading to teachers.
body_markdown:
If you are wondering **how to grade your child’s IB coursework at home** , the safest answer is not to assign an official mark. Instead, conduct a structured **parent review** that checks whether the work is focused, supported, analytical, reflective, clearly presented, and compliant with current requirements.


An Internal Assessment, or **IA** , is subject-specific coursework completed within an IB course. In most subjects, the teacher marks the work before the IB moderates a sample to check how accurately the school has applied the global standard. A home review can reveal gaps your child should investigate, but it cannot reproduce professional teacher judgment or predict a moderated mark precisely.


### What grading IB coursework at home should mean


A parent review is a **diagnostic check** , not unofficial teaching or assessment. You are looking for visible evidence that the relevant criteria might reward, such as a focused question, justified choices, supported analysis, specific evaluation, and clear communication.


Exact criteria, mark totals, formats, and submission rules differ by subject, level, syllabus, and examination session. Ask your child for the rubric and instructions currently used by the school rather than relying on an older guide found online.


The IB’s explanation of[Diploma Programme assessment](https://ibo.org/programmes/diploma-programme/assessment-and-exams/understanding-ib-assessment/) confirms that internally assessed work is marked by teachers and moderated by the IB. Moderation checks whether criteria have been applied consistently, so the school’s marks may remain unchanged or be adjusted.


### Establish the academic-integrity boundary


The essential rule is that **the ideas, decisions, analysis, language, and final work must remain your child’s own** . The IB’s[academic integrity policy](https://www.ibo.org/globalassets/new-structure/programmes/shared-resources/pdfs/academic-integrity-policy-en.pdf) explains that parents can support planning and understanding of policies but must avoid unauthorized assistance with coursework.


A parent may ask neutral questions, discuss time management, notice missing labels, or identify an explanation that is difficult to follow. A parent should not rewrite paragraphs, repair calculations, choose conclusions, find and insert sources, supply analysis, or tell the student exactly what to add. School policies may be stricter, especially after a draft has been authenticated or the permitted teacher-feedback stage has ended.


Appropriate parent support Support that risks crossing the line


Asking the student to explain the research question Rewriting or narrowing the question


Noticing that a graph lacks a title or source Rebuilding the graph or selecting better data


Asking where a factual claim originated Finding sources and inserting citations


Identifying a paragraph that is difficult to follow Rewriting it in stronger academic language


Helping create a deadline calendar Directing academic decisions


Encouraging consultation with the teacher Editing or completing the work


If the boundary is uncertain, consult the subject teacher or DP coordinator first. RevisionDojo’s guide to[supporting IA work without taking over](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/supporting-ia-work) provides further practical guidance for parents.


### Prepare for an IB IA parent review


Before reading, ask your child for:


- The **current task instructions** supplied by the school
- The **current assessment criteria or rubric**
- Any teacher checklist or formatting instructions
- The draft in a form that may be reviewed at this stage


Confirm the subject, level, examination session, deadline, and permitted feedback stage. RevisionDojo’s[subject-specific IA guides](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ia-guides) can clarify terminology, but the school’s current instructions remain authoritative.


Read the complete draft once without commenting. During a second reading, record questions with page or paragraph references. This prevents the review from turning into line-by-line editing and leaves your child responsible for deciding how to respond.


### A step-by-step home review method


The following categories are mapped loosely to qualities commonly assessed in IAs. They are not universal criterion titles, and each subject applies its own requirements.


### Check the task, focus, and purpose


Ask your child to state the investigation’s question or purpose in one sentence without reading the draft. Compare that explanation with the title, introduction, method, analysis, and conclusion.


Check whether the focus is specific enough for the permitted scope, important terms are defined, and every section addresses the same purpose. If the focus appears broad or inconsistent, identify where the problem occurs rather than proposing a replacement question.


### Examine planning and methodological choices


Many IAs reward an appropriate research design, method, selection of sources, or planned approach. The evidence varies by subject: a science investigation may require controlled variables and a replicable procedure, while history may emphasize source selection and evaluation.


Ask, “Why was this choice made?” about major methods, texts, cases, models, data sources, or mathematical techniques. Look for unexplained samples, undefined measurements, unjustified sources, or methods that cannot answer the stated question. Record each gap as a question instead of solving it.


### Separate evidence from analysis


More data, quotations, calculations, or examples do not automatically create stronger analysis. Evidence becomes valuable when the student explains what it shows, how the interpretation was reached, and why it matters to the research question.


Select three important pieces of evidence and ask:


1. What does this evidence show?
2. How do you know?
3. Why does it matter to the question?
4. Is another interpretation possible?


If the answer is unclear, write a neutral note such as, “What conclusion should the reader draw from this table?” Do not provide the missing interpretation.


### Test reasoning and subject understanding


Read the central argument as a sequence of claims. Each major claim should have relevant evidence, an explanation, and a clear connection to the conclusion. Unsupported transitions often appear around words such as “therefore,” “proves,” or “significant.”


A non-specialist can notice a logical gap without correcting technical content. The student should verify formulas, disciplinary terminology, statistical decisions, and subject-specific interpretations against course materials and teacher guidance. RevisionDojo’s explanation of[detailed IB IA feedback](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-internal-assessment-feedback-detailed-comments-and-suggestions) shows why effective feedback identifies observable evidence rather than giving a general impression.


### Review evaluation and reflection


Weak evaluation often lists generic limitations such as “human error” or states that more data would improve reliability. Stronger evaluation identifies a precise weakness, explains its likely effect, and proposes a feasible improvement directly connected to it.


Apply three checks:


- **Specificity:** Is the limitation precisely identified?
- **Consequence:** Is its effect on interpretation or confidence explained?
- **Response:** Is the improvement realistic and relevant?


Where reflection is assessed, ask what changed in the student’s understanding or approach. Reflection should reveal developed thinking rather than merely state that the task was interesting or difficult.


### Check communication and traceability


A reader should be able to follow the work without reconstructing missing steps. Check headings, paragraph order, labels, units, figure and table titles, appendices, and citation consistency.


Also ask whether information, data, quotations, images, and ideas can be traced to their sources. A bibliography alone is insufficient when material is not acknowledged at the relevant point. Flag inconsistencies, but allow your child to correct them independently.


### Apply the rubric without pretending to be an examiner


Read one criterion at a time and identify command terms such as **identifies** , **explains** , **analyses** , **evaluates** , and **justifies** . Ask your child to locate the exact passage that demonstrates each requirement.


Use an evidence map instead of a final grade:


Review category Evidence status Useful parent question


Focus and purpose Clear, partial, or missing Is the same question followed throughout?


Method or approach Clear, partial, or missing Why was this approach appropriate?


Analysis and reasoning Clear, partial, or missing What does this evidence demonstrate?


Evaluation or reflection Clear, partial, or missing What is the effect of this limitation?


Communication Clear, partial, or missing Can the reader trace every source and step?


If you assign provisional marks, use broad ranges and acknowledge uncertainty. Never convert an estimated IA mark directly into a subject grade because component weightings, moderation, grade boundaries, and examination performance also affect the final result.


### Return questions, not a rewritten draft


Limit your final review to **three priority issues** . An extensive list of corrections can distract from weaknesses in methodology, reasoning, analysis, or evaluation.


Useful comments identify a location and a reader’s problem: “On page 3, I could not see why this source was selected,” or “The table is clear, but its pattern is not explained.” Your child must decide whether the observation is valid and how to revise. Questions requiring subject expertise should be taken to the teacher.


Common parent mistakes include rewarding polished prose despite weak analysis, encouraging imitation of an online exemplar, and concentrating on a numerical score. Exemplars may illustrate criteria, but copying their structure, language, data, or ideas can create authenticity concerns. RevisionDojo’s discussion of[diagnostic IB IA grading](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-ia-grading-service-professional-assessment-in-minutes) explains why criterion-level evidence is more useful than a supposedly guaranteed mark.


### When additional support is appropriate


Contact the teacher or DP coordinator if the concern involves task interpretation, methods, authenticity, permitted feedback, or submission rules. The school is the appropriate authority for its procedures and current subject requirements.


Rubric-aware tools can identify possible gaps, but their results remain provisional. RevisionDojo’s[Coursework Grader](https://www.revisiondojo.com/features/coursework-grader) offers criterion-linked feedback, while[Jojo AI and IA support](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/revisiondojo-ia-help) can clarify unfamiliar terminology. Students must verify suggestions against school guidance and use these tools to support their own thinking, not generate submitted work.


### Conclusion


Parents can review IB coursework effectively without acting as examiners. Use the current rubric, look for visible evidence, ask neutral questions, identify no more than three priorities, and protect the student’s ownership of every academic decision and revision.


The goal is not a definitive mark. It is to help your child notice what a reader can and cannot see before seeking authorized guidance. RevisionDojo’s IA guides and Coursework Grader can provide a structured rubric-based check when used alongside teacher feedback and academic-integrity rules.
